transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-22
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Miles (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Alex Reed (Nimbus Platform), Sana Kapoor (Nimbus ML Infra), Tom Li (Nimbus SRE)

Summary (auto): Technical deep dive on throughput tuning for Redwood runtime. Focus areas: continuous batching behavior, scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, max_tokens_in_flight), token limits and tail latency, KV cache warmup, quantization implications for perf, and on-prem/VPC networking considerations. Agreed to run PoC benchmarks with sample traffic and share configs.

Topics: continuous batching; scheduler knobs; max_num_seqs; token limits; KV cache; quantization; VPC/on-prem; bench scripts

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have about an hour, um, for a deep dive on throughput tuning. I'll hand over to Priya for the runtime details.
[00:18] Priya: Thanks Jordan. Hi Alex, Sana, Tom. Quick agenda: continuous batching overview, scheduler knobs you can tune (max_num_seqs, max_batch_tokens, token_in_flight limits), KV cache behavior on long conversations, quantization tradeoffs, and on-prem/VPC networking gotchas. I'll go slow and pause for questions.
[00:36] Alex: Sounds good. Our main ask is to get 1000 reqs/sec at P50 < 120ms for 32-token responses if possible, and understand costs. We mostly run 4k tokens/day per user pattern, mixed short/long.
[00:50] Priya: Right, important to get the request distribution. For continuous batching the runtime keeps an open batch window to accumulate sequences; the trick is balancing the batch latency vs throughput. On GPUs we target 8-16 sequences per batch for our medium models, but depends on seq len.
[01:12] Tom: Quick Q: how does max_num_seqs relate to max_batch_tokens? Are they both limiting the same resource?
[01:24] Priya: Good Q. max_num_seqs is the maximum number of concurrent sequences we will put in a single generation step, it's sequence-count based. max_batch_tokens is token-budget based - if you have many short requests you might hit num_seqs limit first; many long ones you hit batch_tokens first.
[01:48] Sana: Our traffic is bursty during market open; we have lots of short queries (10-20 tokens) and some long ones (200-500 tokens). How to avoid short queries starving long ones?
[02:02] Priya: We expose scheduler priority and soft-degrade policies. For mixed profiles we recommend token-aware scheduling: give long requests slightly higher priority or set a separate queue for long tails. Also setting max_tokens_in_flight helps - it ensures a single request doesn't monopolize GPU memory.
[02:28] Jordan: There's also continuous KV cache warmup behavior to consider. If you have many unique contexts the KV cache hit rate is low and you lose batch efficiency.
[02:40] Alex: We're storing per-user conversation state, but many sessions are single-turn. That means the KV cache won't be reused much. What's the practical impact?
[02:52] Priya: If KV cache misses are high, we do full forward passes each time which increases compute per token and reduces effective throughput. For your workload, enabling prefix caching and shorter session window (like last 4 turns) can help. Also warmup preloads - running a background batch to populate cache for common prompts can reduce first-token latency.
[03:20] Tom: Is there any danger in preloading? Network costs or staleness?
[03:28] Priya: Preloading is safe if prompts are stable; for dynamic content we recommend TTL-based cache invalidation. There is minor extra compute cost but you gain P50 & P95 improvements.
[03:40] Sana: Let's talk quantization. We're evaluating 4-bit quant models. How much reg does that buy us and what are the perf tradeoffs?
[03:52] Priya: 4-bit (Q4) often halves memory footprint versus FP16 and gives better packing for throughput. However quantization can change kernel selection - some kernels are optimized poorly on certain GPUs and may increase latency for small batch sizes. For large-batch throughput it usually helps. Our recommendation: run benchmarks with your seq distribution.
[04:16] Alex: Do we need to tweak scheduler knobs differently for quantized models?
[04:22] Priya: Yes, quantized execution tends to be more memory-bound but compute-efficient. You might raise max_num_seqs slightly since memory per seq is lower, but monitor tail latency.
[04:34] [05:00] Jordan: I'll pause - any quick clarifying Qs?
[05:10] Alex: Can you explain continuous batching window sizes? We saw a config called batch_wait_ms in your docs.
[05:18] Priya: batch_wait_ms controls how long the runtime holds an in-flight batch waiting for more requests. Lower makes latency better but reduces batch fullness. For bursty patterns, 5-10ms is common; for steady throughput you can go up to 20-50ms to increase GPU efficiency. The tradeoff is added tail-latency for early requests.
[05:44] Tom: Our SLO is strict - we can't add more than 30ms P50. So 50ms is too big.
[05:50] Priya: Understood - then keep batch_wait_ms low and focus on increasing concurrency (more callers) and max_num_seqs to fill batches from parallel inflight requests. Also continuous batching works best when many in-flight connections hammer the endpoint.
[06:06] Alex: What about max_num_seqs practical numbers? For our A100 80GB, what should we set?
[06:12] Priya: For A100 80GB with Q4 and medium-sized 20B-ish models, we see good throughput at max_num_seqs=32-48 and max_batch_tokens around 32k-48k, but that depends on sequence lengths. For 4k context windows you'll need to consider KV cache memory.
[06:36] Sana: We don't want to push memory too hard - we run multiple workers per node. Any orchestration tips?
[06:44] Priya: Yes, split model shards across GPUs or use model parallel pools; dedicate some GPUs for long-context requests. You can also configure per-route limits so heavy long-context routes don't starve short routes.
[06:58] Alex: On the networking side for VPC/private deployments - any latency we should expect from internal routing? Does a NAT/gateway add tail latency?
[07:08] Priya: If you're on VPC or on-prem, ensure the control-plane to data-plane RTT is low and avoid unnecessary proxies. Sidecar proxies or heavy L7 routing can add 5-20ms. For strict SLOs we recommend colocating clients in the same AZ and using direct paths; also enable TCP keepalive to prevent cold-start connection overhead.
[07:30] Tom: Ok. Can you walk through what a tuning workflow looks like?
[07:36] Priya: Sure - step 1: gather request distribution (tokens per req, concurrency). Step 2: run synthetic bench with your distribution against a small pool (1-2 GPUs) with logging of per-token latencies. Step 3: iterate on knobs: batch_wait_ms, max_num_seqs, max_batch_tokens, max_tokens_in_flight. Step 4: try quantization variants. Step 5: scale out and test autoscale. We'll share a benchmark repo.
[08:08] Alex: We can provide token histograms. We'll need a reference bench script.
[08:14] Jordan: We'll share the bench repo and a sample config.
[08:18] [08:25] Sana: How do we interpret max_tokens_in_flight? Is that per sequence or across batch?
[08:32] Priya: It's across the worker - it caps total tokens being processed concurrently which prevents OOM from a few long requests. It's a global in-flight token counter for the scheduler.
[08:44] Tom: If a request would exceed the limit, does it queue or fail?
[08:48] Priya: It queues with a timeout by default; you can configure hard rejects if you prefer immediate failure. For user-facing APIs we usually queue with a short timeout.
[08:58] Alex: Any autoscaling interplay? If we queue too much we might trigger scale-up slower.
[09:04] Priya: Right - tune autoscale to react on queue depth as well as GPU utilization. We provide metrics for queued requests and token/backlog.
[09:14] Alex: Let's talk about tail latency mitigation. We saw an old note on prioritized batching - is that available?
[09:22] Priya: Yes, prioritized queues allow short requests to skip or be batched separately. You can also set per-route max_batch_tokens to ensure short paths remain fast. Combining small batch windows and a short-priority queue keeps P95 down.
[09:38] Jordan: Another trick is warm-start: keep some reserved capacity (dedicated pool) for spike protection while letting autoscale handle baseline.
[09:46] Sana: For on-prem we may not want reserved spare GPUs. Any suggestions for cost-constrained environments?
[09:54] Priya: Use mixed precision and aggressive quantization; set conservative max_tokens_in_flight and tighter request timeouts, and consider burst proxying to hosted Redwood for overflow (hybrid).
[10:08] Alex: We are evaluating hybrid - what are the security implications of overflow to hosted?
[10:14] Jordan: Data residency and encryption are key. We can do blind mode or use field-level encryption; also we have private deployments option if required. We'll share security docs.
[10:26] [10:30] Tom: Back to scheduling knobs - can you give example config snippets?
[10:34] Priya: Sure - sample: max_num_seqs: 32, max_batch_tokens: 32000, batch_wait_ms: 10, max_tokens_in_flight: 64000. For Q4 on A100 you might bump max_num_seqs to 48. We'll attach these in the repo.
[10:56] Alex: If we increase max_num_seqs, does that negatively affect latency for single requests due to larger kernel latency?
[11:02] Priya: There can be a small penalty for first token if kernel launch overhead increases, but overall per-token cost drops. For strict single-request latency, keep a small priority queue.
[11:12] Sana: Any gotchas with KV cache eviction when max_num_seqs is high?
[11:18] Priya: With more sequences, cache control is more important - you might reach memory limits and eviction frequency increases. Monitor cache hit rates; if eviction thrashes you should lower max_num_seqs or use quantization to free memory.
[11:34] Alex: What observability do you recommend during bench runs?
[11:38] Priya: Collect per-token latency, GPU utilization, memory used, batch fullness, queue depth, KV cache hit ratio, and kernel types. We expose these in the console and via Prometheus.
[11:52] Tom: Can we export metrics to our Grafana?
[11:56] Jordan: Yes - we can push Prometheus metrics and a sample dashboard.
[12:00] [12:05] Sana: A corner case - multipart requests where a user sends 1k tokens followed by several small followups in quick succession; any special handling?
[12:14] Priya: Best to treat the long one in a separate long-context route or use chunking; also you can enable streaming so partial tokens return sooner while the rest compute. Streaming reduces perceived latency for users.
[12:30] Alex: You mentioned kernel selection earlier. Is that automatic?
[12:34] Priya: Yes the runtime picks kernels based on model shape, quantization, and seq len; you can force a kernel choice for experimentation but it's advanced. Usually let the runtime auto-select.
[12:46] [13:00] Jordan: Quick pause for a questions queue - Alex?
[13:04] Alex: How do you recommend scaling from single-node perf numbers to k nodes? Linear? less?
[13:10] Priya: Throughput should scale near-linearly for independent requests, but you'll see sub-linear scaling due to network and scheduling overhead. For small-batch scenarios expect diminishing returns; for large-batch steady traffic scaling is close to linear. Also watch for double-counted KV caches across nodes; using shared cache can help but adds complexity.
[13:34] Tom: Do you support shared KV cache across workers?
[13:38] Priya: We have experimental shared-KV features; it helps hit rates but requires low-latency networking between workers. For on-prem with RDMA it's beneficial.
[13:50] Sana: Ok, let's go through a concrete tuning example for our profile - mostly 12-token queries at 1200 reqs/sec bursts, plus 1% long 400-token requests.
[14:02] Priya: For that mix I'd suggest: batch_wait_ms=8ms, max_num_seqs=24-32, max_batch_tokens=16000, max_tokens_in_flight=48000, prioritize short-queue with 30% of capacity. For A100 Q4 you might nudge num_seqs +8. Also set short-request timeouts of 200ms.
[14:34] Alex: If we do that, what P50/P95 improvements can we expect?
[14:38] Priya: Based on similar customers, P50 for short requests can be ~20-40ms and P95 under 120ms at target throughput when tuned. But benchmarks are needed.
[14:54] Jordan: We'll give you baseline run artifacts, you can compare after your runs.
[15:00] [15:08] Alex: Any memory calculations docs you can share for max_num_seqs vs context length?
[15:12] Priya: Yes - we have heuristics: memory ~ base_model_mem + per_seq_mem * max_num_seqs + kv_cache_mem * context_length * active_sessions. We'll share a worksheet.
[15:30] Tom: For the worksheet, please show examples for A100 80GB and H100 80GB.
[15:36] Priya: Will do. H100 behavior differs with kernel availability; some kernels perform better on H100.
[15:44] Alex: Any pitfalls with mixed-precision + quant? We tried Q2/3 in house and saw quality regressions.
[15:52] Priya: Quality should be validated with evals. Quantization-aware finetuning or LLM-int8-runtime (LIR) techniques often reduce regressions. We recommend running your eval prompts. Redwood Optimize can help suggest profiles.
[16:08] Sana: Will Redwood support dynamic quantization switching per route?
[16:14] Priya: We support model variants per route; you can route some traffic to Q4 and some to FP16. That helps keep critical paths on higher-fidelity models.
[16:26] [16:30] Jordan: Someone asked earlier about kernel launch overhead with larger batches; for very small latency-sensitive requests, sometimes batching is detrimental. That's why prioritized small-queue is helpful.
[16:40] Alex: For our 1% long requests, would separate pool be overkill?
[16:46] Priya: Not necessarily - a small dedicated pool for long-context could simplify tuning and avoid interference. Cost tradeoff vs complexity to manage.
[16:56] Tom: What about autoscaling cooldowns - any recommended settings?
[17:00] Priya: Use short cooldowns for scale-up (30-60s) and longer for scale-down (5-10 min) to avoid flapping. Trigger on GPU util and queue depth.
[17:12] Alex: Can Redwood expose per-request trace IDs for later correlation?
[17:16] Jordan: Yes we attach request IDs and you can trace them in the console; we also export to tracing backends.
[17:24] Sana: Any security implication of attaching full request bodies to traces?
[17:28] Jordan: We mask or allow redaction; we can disable payload logging for PII. We'll send the security checklist.
[17:36] [17:45] Alex: Ok, quick walk through of the PoC we'd run - what do you need from us?
[17:50] Priya: Token histogram, typical concurrency, a few representative prompts, and network topology (VPC peering, proxies). We'll run bench harness with those and iterate configs.
[18:06] Alex: We'll prepare that next 48 hours.
[18:10] Jordan: Great. Any last perf nitty-gritty?
[18:14] Priya: One more: for batching drivers we instrument batch fullness metric - if you see under 40% fullness consider increasing concurrency or batch_wait_ms. Also watch for imbalanced batch composition when request lengths vary.
[18:30] Tom: For on-prem RDMA note - is there recommended MTU or kernel tuning?
[18:36] Priya: Use jumbo frames and tune TCP buffer sizes; we'll share a networking checklist.
[18:44] Alex: Competitor question - do others provide prioritized queues out-of-box? We looked at Anthropic and Bedrock.
[18:52] Jordan: Some cloud providers have simpler FIFO endpoints; Redwood emphasizes per-route scheduling and prioritized queues as part of the offering. We'll provide a short comparison doc.
[19:06] Sana: Let's capture concrete action items.
[19:10] Jordan: Sure.
[19:12] Priya: Action items recap: 1) Priya to share bench repo + example configs + kernel notes. 2) Jordan to send security docs & VPC checklist. 3) Alex to send token histograms and sample prompts. 4) Schedule follow-up PoC run for next week.
[19:34] Alex: That aligns.
[19:38] Tom: Thanks folks.
[19:40] Jordan: Thanks all - we'll follow up by end of day with artifacts.
[19:44] [19:50] END OF TRANSCRIPT
